title: Serverless Application Development
learning_outcomes: Explain the purpose of serverless application development and its relationship to AWS Serverless Computing.
Interpret the example and identify at least one prerequisite or boundary relevant to serverless application development.
Propose a safe verification or troubleshooting step and record one security, reliability or cost consideration.

content.intro: In this lesson, you will learn serverless application development in the context of AWS Serverless Computing. You will connect the listed subtopics to a practical decision, inspect a small example, and define evidence that would confirm or disprove your assumptions.
content.why_it_matters: Serverless Application Development matters because it is one part of aws lambda and serverless computing. Real workloads depend on explicit prerequisites, correct permissions, predictable behavior and a way to verify outcomes. Learning the decision points helps you distinguish a working demonstration from a safe and supportable design.

content_blocks.title: Event-driven application path
content_blocks.alt_text: An event is validated, routed to a function or worker, persisted or acknowledged, and observed; retries and dead-letter handling cover failures.
content_blocks.caption: Assume messages can be delivered more than once; design idempotent consumers.

content_blocks.title: Core idea
content_blocks.text:
**Core idea.** Serverless Application Development belongs to AWS Serverless Computing. Serverless removes server management, not architecture work. Design execution roles, event contracts, timeouts, concurrency, retries, idempotency and observability.

The PDF lists these subtopics: AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM); Local development and testing; Deployment configuration; Managing application environments. Treat them as a connected workflow rather than a list to memorize. Start with the workload requirement, identify the AWS resource/control involved, and write down who owns configuration and operation.

content_blocks.title: Practical reasoning
content_blocks.text: **Apply it safely.** For serverless application development, name the prerequisites and the expected result before making a change. Prefer a read-only inspection or local/static example first. Then plan a normal case, a failure case, and a verification step. In a live account, require the account owner-approved sandbox, narrow permissions, spend visibility and cleanup plan. Do not put credentials in code or commit local configuration files.

items.title: AWS Serverless Application Model (AWS SAM)
items.text: Define the input/data permissions, expected evidence, evaluation cases, safety boundaries and cost limits. A generated answer or completed invocation is not by itself proof of correctness.

items.title: Local development and testing
items.text: Compare the available option with the workload requirement; record the operational, security, availability and cost trade-offs rather than assuming one option is always best.

items.title: Deployment configuration
items.text: Keep the workflow repeatable and reviewable: version the input, validate before applying, inspect changes, protect state/secrets, and specify how to roll back.

items.title: Managing application environments
items.text: Record ownership, dependencies and teardown/recovery behavior so the design can be operated safely after the first successful test.

content_blocks.title: Minimal Lambda handler: Serverless Application Development
content_blocks.expected_output: Given {"name":"Ari"}, the handler returns a statusCode of 200 and body "Hello, Ari!"; this is a local illustration, not an AWS deployment.
content_blocks.run_instructions: This block is an inspectable example, not an AWS action performed by CodeLeaf. Review the example as text and adapt it only after checking current official service documentation. Do not apply/deploy changes in a real account without account-owner approval, least-privilege permissions and a reviewed cost/cleanup plan.
content_blocks.reset_steps: No AWS resource is created by this lesson example. If you independently run an approved lab, capture the starting state first, follow the lab-specific teardown instructions, check dependent resources and billing/resource inventories, and document anything retained.
content_blocks.limitations: The CodeLeaf playground is an HTML/CSS/JavaScript preview and does not execute AWS APIs, shell commands, SQL or cloud deployments. Treat output as illustrative; live values depend on credentials, permissions, Region, service state and schema.

content_blocks.title: Security and cost checkpoint
content_blocks.text: Use least privilege, keep Block Public Access/private defaults unless a justified reviewed requirement says otherwise, and document cost/cleanup before live changes.

task: Create a one-page decision card for “Serverless Application Development”. State the goal, prerequisites, the AWS resource or control involved, the expected result, one read-only/static verification step, one failure case, the relevant permission boundary, and cost/cleanup considerations. Do not create or alter billable resources unless the account owner has approved the lab.
hints: Start from the exact subtopics in the lesson and define the desired state in your own words.
Prefer a read-only check or static artifact before a mutating command; record the identity/Region and required permissions.
Verify the expected result and a failure path using current official documentation; write down cost and cleanup implications.
expected_output: A short reviewable decision card for Serverless Application Development with prerequisites, evidence, a failure case, security implications and cost/cleanup notes.

common_mistakes.problem: Treating one successful example as proof of production readiness.
common_mistakes.why: The example may not test permissions, regional/service prerequisites, retries, recovery, quotas or edge cases.
common_mistakes.fix: Write acceptance criteria, test a failure path, inspect logs/state and record the limits of the result.

common_mistakes.problem: Changing a live resource before confirming its effect and cost.
common_mistakes.why: Cloud changes can expose data, break traffic or leave billable dependencies behind.
common_mistakes.fix: Start read-only, use an approved sandbox, review the change, tag ownership and verify cleanup.

common_mistakes.problem: Copying broad permissions or credentials into source files.
common_mistakes.why: Broad permissions and leaked long-lived credentials increase the impact of mistakes.
common_mistakes.fix: Use scoped roles/temporary credentials, keep secrets in approved stores and review access boundaries.

summary: Serverless Application Development is taught as part of AWS Serverless Computing.
Serverless removes server management, not architecture work. Design execution roles, event contracts, timeouts, concurrency, retries, idempotency and observability.
Verify assumptions with official service documentation and evidence from the relevant AWS resource, logs or tests.
For live labs, confirm permissions and likely charges before acting, then verify cleanup.
